title: Fence Calculator
metaTitle: Fence Calculator: Posts, Rails, and Pickets Needed
metaDescription: Calculate how many fence posts, rails, and pickets you need for wood privacy fences or pre-built panels with gate and corner allowances.

constants.label: Post spacing (feet)
constants.note: Standard fence post spacing is 8 feet on center. In high-wind areas, 6-foot spacing is recommended. Check local building codes.

constants.label: Pre-built panel width (feet)
constants.note: Most pre-fabricated wood and vinyl fence panels are 8 feet wide (some are 6 feet). Verify with panel manufacturer.

constants.label: Horizontal rails per section
constants.note: Fences 6 feet tall or higher require 3 horizontal 2×4 rails to prevent warping. 4-foot fences typically use 2 rails.

constants.label: Pickets per linear foot
constants.note: Standard 5.5-inch dog-ear pickets with small spacing gaps equal roughly 2.2 to 2.25 pickets per linear foot.

content.intro: Building a wood privacy fence or installing pre-assembled perimeter panels secures your yard, protects children and pets, and establishes clear property boundaries. Estimating fencing materials accurately ensures you buy matching posts, horizontal 2-by-4 rails, and dog-ear pickets without running out mid-installation or paying for surplus lumber. This calculator determines the total post count, pre-assembled panel requirements, horizontal rails, and individual vertical pickets needed based on your total run length. Enter your fence dimensions below to account for gate openings and corner posts, ensuring a sturdy, well-spaced boundary fence.
content.howItWorks: Base post count is calculated by dividing total fence run length by on-center post spacing (typically 8 feet), rounding up to the nearest section, and adding 1 end post. Extra posts are then added for gate latch sides and corner changes. If using pre-assembled fence panels, panel count equals total length divided by panel width, rounded up. For stick-built fences, horizontal rails equal total sections multiplied by the rails per section (typically 3 for a 6-foot fence), while pickets equal length multiplied by pickets per foot (approximately 2.25 for 5.5-inch boards).

examples.title: A 100-foot privacy fence run with 8-foot spacing
examples.text: For a continuous 100-foot fence line without gates: 100 ÷ 8 = 12.5 sections, which rounds up to 13 sections. Base posts equal 13 + 1 = 14 posts. If buying pre-assembled panels, purchase 13 panels. For a custom stick-built fence with 3 rails per section, buy 13 × 3 = 39 rails and 100 × 2.25 = 225 dog-ear pickets.

examples.title: A 120-foot perimeter fence with 1 gate and 2 corners
examples.text: For 120 feet: 120 ÷ 8 = 15 sections. Base post count is 15 + 1 = 16 posts. Adding 1 extra post for gate hanging and 2 corner posts totals 19 posts. Pre-built panel count is 15 panels.

commonMistakes: Spacing posts more than 8 feet apart, causing horizontal rails to sag and pickets to bow under heavy wind.
Using only 2 horizontal rails on a 6-foot privacy fence instead of 3, leading to warped, curled pickets.
Neglecting gate hinge and latch posts, which require heavy-duty 4x6 or 6x6 posts to prevent gate sagging.
Fastening pickets with electro-galvanized drywall screws that rust and leave dark black streaks on cedar or treated pine.

faq.q: What size lumber should I use for fence posts?
faq.a: For standard residential fences up to 6 feet high, pressure-treated 4 × 4 inch lumber rated for Ground Contact (UC4A) is the industry standard. For gate hinge posts or fences 8 feet tall, upgrade to 6 × 6 inch posts to resist sagging and heavy wind loads.

faq.q: How many bags of concrete do I need per fence post?
faq.a: Most residential 4 × 4 posts set in a 10-inch diameter by 36-inch deep hole require approximately three to four 80-pound bags of concrete (or four to five 60-pound bags) per post.
No, keep pickets 1 to 2 inches above the ground level. Allowing wood pickets to contact soil or grass causes rapid moisture absorption, rot, and termite damage.

faq.q: What fasteners are best for building wood fences?
faq.a: Always use hot-dipped galvanized (HDG) or exterior polymer-coated ceramic screws, or stainless steel ring-shank nails. Never use interior zinc-plated drywall screws or electro-galvanized nails, which corrode quickly when exposed to treated lumber chemicals.
